claim: A previous study analyzed protein abundance changes across a 'minimally perturbed' cell cycle by using centrifugal elutriation to differentially enrich distinct cell cycle phases in human NB4 cells.
source: Previously, we analyzed protein abundance changes across a 'minimally perturbed' cell cycle by using centrifugal elutriation to differentially enrich distinct cell cycle phases in human NB4 cells (Ly et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ly et al., 2014.

claim: A large fraction of the proteome changes detected in arrested cells reflect arrest-specific responses rather than physiological cell cycle regulation.
source: While elutriated and arrested cells have similar patterns of DNA content and cyclin expression, a large fraction of the proteome changes detected in arrested cells are found to reflect arrest-specific responses (i.e., starvation, DNA damage, CDK1 inhibition), rather than physiological cell cycle regulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the comparative analysis of data from elutriated and arrested cells presented in the manuscript.

claim: Most cells arrested in G2 by CDK1 inhibition express abnormally high levels of replication and origin licensing factors.
source: For example, we show most cells arrested in G2 by CDK1 inhibition express abnormally high levels of replication and origin licensing factors and are likely poised for genome re-replication.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data and immunofluorescence flow cytometry measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cells arrested in G2 by CDK1 inhibition are likely poised for genome re-replication.
source: For example, we show most cells arrested in G2 by CDK1 inhibition express abnormally high levels of replication and origin licensing factors and are likely poised for genome re-replication.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed high levels of replication and origin licensing factors.

claim: The protein data are available in the Encyclopedia of Proteome Dynamics at http://www.peptracker.com/epd/.
source: The protein data are available in the Encyclopedia of Proteome Dynamics (http://www.peptracker.com/epd/), an online, searchable resource.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about data availability.

claim: Centrifugal elutriation was used to size-separate asynchronously growing cells into populations differentially enriched in distinct phases of the cell cycle.
source: To minimize effects on proteins caused by stress responses that do not reflect physiological regulation specific to cell cycle progression, we used centrifugal elutriation to size-separate asynchronously growing cells into populations differentially enriched in distinct phases of the cell cycle.
evidence: The claim describes the methodology used in the previous study.

claim: The elutriation approach identifies a smaller proportion of genes (~4%) that encode proteins whose abundance is cell cycle regulated than have been reported in previous studies.
source: In particular, the elutriation approach identifies a smaller proportion of genes (∼4%) that encode proteins whose abundance is cell cycle regulated than have been reported in previous studies.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previous studies.

claim: Cell synchronization procedures based upon metabolic and biochemical treatments that arrest cell cycle progression have been more widely used to study cell cycle regulation in mammalian cells than physical methods of separation like elutriation.
source: Cell synchronization procedures, based upon metabolic and biochemical treatments that arrest cell cycle progression (including arrest-release protocols), have been more widely used to study cell cycle regulation in mammalian cells than physical methods of separation, like elutriation.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge of the field.

claim: Arrest methods have potential advantages, including the ease of reproducibly achieving high synchronicity.
source: Arrest methods have potential advantages, including the ease of reproducibly achieving high synchronicity.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about arrest methods.

claim: A major unresolved issue is the extent to which the effects of stress and metabolic perturbation arising from treatments used to cause cell cycle arrest may contribute to observed changes in protein expression unrelated to physiologically relevant cell cycle changes.
source: However, a major unresolved issue is the extent to which the effects of stress and metabolic perturbation, arising from the treatments used to cause cell cycle arrest, may contribute to any observed changes in protein expression unrelated to physiologically relevant cell cycle changes (Shedden and Cooper, 2002; Cooper, 2005; Cooper et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work discussing this issue.

claim: Hydroxyurea depletes deoxynucleotide pools thereby slowing replication.
source: Hydroxyurea depletes deoxynucleotide pools thereby slowing replication, and at high doses, arrests cells at the G1/S border (Young and Hodas, 1964).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Young and Hodas, 1964.

claim: At high doses, hydroxyurea arrests cells at the G1/S border.
source: Hydroxyurea depletes deoxynucleotide pools thereby slowing replication, and at high doses, arrests cells at the G1/S border (Young and Hodas, 1964).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Young and Hodas, 1964.

claim: Serum starvation arrests cells in a state with 2N DNA content.
source: Serum starvation arrests cells in a state with 2N DNA content (Zetterberg et al., 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zetterberg et al., 1982.

claim: High concentrations and prolonged treatment with hydroxyurea can induce replication stress and DNA damage.
source: In the case of hydroxyurea, high concentrations and prolonged treatment can induce replication stress and DNA damage (Saintigny et al., 2001; Alvino et al., 2007; Petermann et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Saintigny et al., 2001; Alvino et al., 2007; Petermann et al., 2010.

claim: Serum starvation induces reversible cell cycle exit, with cells entering a quiescent state (G0 phase).
source: Serum starvation induces reversible cell cycle exit, with cells entering a quiescent state (G0 phase) (Pardee, 1974; O'Farrell, 2011) that is characterized by changes in protein signaling, for example, pRb phosphorylation (Chen et al., 1989), and activation of proteins that inhibit CDK activity, for example, p21 (Cheng et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pardee, 1974; O'Farrell, 2011.

claim: The G0 state induced by serum starvation is characterized by changes in protein signaling, for example, pRb phosphorylation.
source: Serum starvation induces reversible cell cycle exit, with cells entering a quiescent state (G0 phase) (Pardee, 1974; O'Farrell, 2011) that is characterized by changes in protein signaling, for example, pRb phosphorylation (Chen et al., 1989), and activation of proteins that inhibit CDK activity, for example, p21 (Cheng et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 1989.

claim: The G0 state induced by serum starvation is characterized by activation of proteins that inhibit CDK activity, for example, p21.
source: Serum starvation induces reversible cell cycle exit, with cells entering a quiescent state (G0 phase) (Pardee, 1974; O'Farrell, 2011) that is characterized by changes in protein signaling, for example, pRb phosphorylation (Chen et al., 1989), and activation of proteins that inhibit CDK activity, for example, p21 (Cheng et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cheng et al., 2000.

claim: Recent studies showed that the G0 state is transiently populated, even in proliferating cells cultured in serum.
source: Recent studies showed that the G0 state is transiently populated, even in proliferating cells cultured in serum (Spencer et al., 2013; Naetar et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Spencer et al., 2013; Naetar et al., 2014.

claim: The transient population of the G0 state in proliferating cells occurs in an apparently stochastic, but p21-dependent, manner.
source: This occurs in an apparently stochastic, but p21-dependent, manner (Spencer et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Spencer et al., 2013.

claim: Microarray analyses of serum-starved mouse 3T3 cells show that up to ~5% of the probe set changes by ≥1.5-fold.
source: Additionally, microarray analyses of serum-starved mouse 3T3 cells show that up to ∼5% of the probe set changes by ≥1.5-fold (Oki et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Oki et al., 2014.

claim: All experiments have been performed on the same NB4 cell line, grown and analyzed using the same equipment and culture conditions to facilitate comparison between arrested and elutriated cell populations.
source: To facilitate the comparison between these arrested cell populations and our previous analysis of the 'minimally perturbed' cell cycle using elutriated cells, all experiments have been performed on the same NB4 cell line (Lanotte et al., 1991), grown, and analysed using the same equipment and culture conditions.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design to ensure comparability.

claim: The NB4 cell line was established from long-term cultures of acute myeloid leukemia blast cells grown on bone-marrow stromal fibroblasts.
source: To facilitate the comparison between these arrested cell populations and our previous analysis of the 'minimally perturbed' cell cycle using elutriated cells, all experiments have been performed on the same NB4 cell line (Lanotte et al., 1991), grown, and analysed using the same equipment and culture conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lanotte et al., 1991.

claim: Serum starvation for 48 hr was used to arrest cells in G0/G1 phase.
source: Serum starvation for 48 hr was used to arrest cells in G0/G1 phase.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental method used.

claim: Cells were treated with hydroxyurea for 18 hr to arrest cells in S phase.
source: To arrest cells in S phase, cells were treated with hydroxyurea for 18 hr.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental method used.

claim: Cells were treated with RO-3306 for 18 hr to arrest cells in G2 phase.
source: To arrest cells in G2 phase, cells were treated with RO-3306 for 18 hr, which specifically inhibits CDK1 activity and arrests cells at the G2/M border (Vassilev et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental method used.

claim: RO-3306 specifically inhibits CDK1 activity and arrests cells at the G2/M border.
source: To arrest cells in G2 phase, cells were treated with RO-3306 for 18 hr, which specifically inhibits CDK1 activity and arrests cells at the G2/M border (Vassilev et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vassilev et al., 2006.

claim: Each experiment was performed in biological triplicate.
source: Each experiment was performed in biological triplicate.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design.

claim: Flow cytometry analysis of DNA content and immunoblot analysis of established cell cycle markers confirmed that the respective serum starvation, hydroxyurea, and RO-3306 treatments each arrested NB4 cells at the expected cell cycle phase.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of DNA content and immunoblot analysis of established cell cycle markers confirmed that the respective serum starvation (SS), hydroxyurea (HU), and RO-3306 treatments each arrested NB4 cells at the expected cell cycle phase (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Serum starvation increases the frequency of 2N DNA content cells (G0/G1 arrest).
source: Thus, the DNA content profiles show that SS increases the frequency of 2N DNA content cells (G0/G1 arrest), HU increases the frequency of cells between 2N and 4N DNA content (S arrest), and RO-3306 increases the frequency of 4N DNA content cells (G2 arrest) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Hydroxyurea increases the frequency of cells between 2N and 4N DNA content (S arrest).
source: Thus, the DNA content profiles show that SS increases the frequency of 2N DNA content cells (G0/G1 arrest), HU increases the frequency of cells between 2N and 4N DNA content (S arrest), and RO-3306 increases the frequency of 4N DNA content cells (G2 arrest) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RO-3306 increases the frequency of 4N DNA content cells (G2 arrest).
source: Thus, the DNA content profiles show that SS increases the frequency of 2N DNA content cells (G0/G1 arrest), HU increases the frequency of cells between 2N and 4N DNA content (S arrest), and RO-3306 increases the frequency of 4N DNA content cells (G2 arrest) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: NB4 cells appear hypersensitive to hydroxyurea and undergo apoptosis at concentrations typically used to arrest other cell lines (i.e., 1–5 mM vs 80 μM in this study).
source: Interestingly, NB4 cells appear hypersensitive to hydroxyurea and undergo apoptosis at concentrations typically used to arrest other cell lines (i.e., 1–5 mM vs 80 μM in this study).
evidence: The claim is based on observations made during the study.

claim: RO-3306 can induce genome re-replication.
source: RO-3306, which can induce genome re-replication (Vassilev et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2009), induces re-replication in ∼3.3% of treated NB4 cells (cells with >4N DNA content in Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vassilev et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2009.

claim: RO-3306 induces re-replication in ~3.3% of treated NB4 cells.
source: RO-3306, which can induce genome re-replication (Vassilev et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2009), induces re-replication in ∼3.3% of treated NB4 cells (cells with >4N DNA content in Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The abundance profiles of cyclin E and cyclin A both peak in S-arrested cells.
source: As shown in Figure 1C, the abundance profiles of cyclin E and cyclin A, which both peak in S-arrested cells, and cyclin B1, which peaks in G2-arrested cells, are consistent with the reported cell cycle regulation for these proteins (Pines and Hunter, 1989; Pines, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cyclin B1 peaks in G2-arrested cells.
source: As shown in Figure 1C, the abundance profiles of cyclin E and cyclin A, which both peak in S-arrested cells, and cyclin B1, which peaks in G2-arrested cells, are consistent with the reported cell cycle regulation for these proteins (Pines and Hunter, 1989; Pines, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The abundance profiles of cyclin E, cyclin A, and cyclin B1 are consistent with the reported cell cycle regulation for these proteins.
source: As shown in Figure 1C, the abundance profiles of cyclin E and cyclin A, which both peak in S-arrested cells, and cyclin B1, which peaks in G2-arrested cells, are consistent with the reported cell cycle regulation for these proteins (Pines and Hunter, 1989; Pines, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pines and Hunter, 1989; Pines, 1999 and data in Figure 1C.

claim: The arrested NB4 cell populations show high enrichment for the targeted cell cycle phases.
source: In summary, the DNA content and immunoblot analyses indicate that the arrested NB4 cell populations show high enrichment for the targeted cell cycle phases.
evidence: The claim is based on the DNA content and immunoblot analyses presented.

claim: The enrichment profiles obtained by arrest are similar to those obtained by centrifugal elutriation.
source: Moreover, the enrichment profiles obtained by arrest are similar to those obtained by centrifugal elutriation (cf. [Ly et al., 2014] Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with data from Ly et al., 2014.

claim: Any differences observed in protein abundance between cell cycle phases in the respective arrested and elutriated samples will not be due primarily to differences in enrichment efficiency.
source: Therefore, any differences observed in protein abundance between cell cycle phases in the respective arrested and elutriated samples will not be due primarily to differences in enrichment efficiency.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the similar enrichment profiles.

claim: In total, 46,783 peptides were identified, corresponding to 4,339 proteins identified with two or more peptides per protein.
source: In total, 46,783 peptides were identified, corresponding to 4,339 proteins identified with two or more peptides per protein (submitted to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository, accession PXD001610).
evidence: The claim reports the results of the proteomic analysis.

claim: Comparison of the label-free quantitative (LFQ) intensities between all three biological replicates reveals a high positive correlation (>0.95) in all cases.
source: Comparison of the label-free quantitative (LFQ) intensities (Cox 2014) between all three biological replicates, (Figure 1D), reveals a high positive correlation (>0.95) in all cases, indicating that the intensities measured are reproducibly quantitated.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The high positive correlation (>0.95) between biological replicates indicates that the intensities measured are reproducibly quantitated.
source: Comparison of the label-free quantitative (LFQ) intensities (Cox 2014) between all three biological replicates, (Figure 1D), reveals a high positive correlation (>0.95) in all cases, indicating that the intensities measured are reproducibly quantitated.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the high correlation observed.

claim: The final proteomic dataset after quality control filtering consisted of 3,068 proteins identified with two or more peptides per protein and quantitated in all three replicates within a treatment group.
source: The data were filtered further to include only those proteins that were detected in all three replicates within a treatment group. This produces a high quality data set comprising 3,068 proteins that were used to evaluate changes in protein abundance in the respective arrested cell populations (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim describes the final dataset after filtering.

claim: A protein was classified as regulated by cell cycle arrest when the protein abundance change was ≥twofold between any two conditions.
source: As in the elutriated cell study (Ly et al., 2014), a protein was classified as regulated by cell cycle arrest when the protein abundance change was ≥twofold between any two conditions.
evidence: The claim describes the criteria used for classification.

claim: The statistical robustness of the measured fold changes in the arrest data set was determined using a one-way ANOVA and a p-value cutoff of 0.05 was implemented.
source: The statistical robustness of the measured fold changes in the arrest data set was determined using a one-way ANOVA and a p-value cutoff of 0.05 was implemented.
evidence: The claim describes the statistical method used.

claim: Based on multiple criteria, including multiple supportive sequence-unique peptides, biological reproducibility, and effect size, 484 proteins were deemed cell cycle arrest regulated.
source: Thus, based on multiple criteria, including multiple supportive sequence-unique peptides, biological reproducibility, and effect size, 484 proteins were deemed cell cycle arrest regulated (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim reports the number of proteins identified as cell cycle arrest regulated.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of the 484 arrest regulated proteins identified four clusters, each showing peak protein abundance at different cell cycle phases.
source: The abundances of these 484 arrest regulated proteins were scaled to have the same mean and standard deviation, and the patterns grouped by hierarchal clustering and illustrated using a heatmap (Figure 2A). This identified four clusters (Figure 2B,C), each showing peak protein abundance at different cell cycle phases, that is, proteins that peak in G0/G1 (12%), S(40%), and G2(22%) arrested cells, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A, B, C.

claim: 12% of the arrest regulated proteins peak in G0/G1 arrested cells.
source: This identified four clusters (Figure 2B,C), each showing peak protein abundance at different cell cycle phases, that is, proteins that peak in G0/G1 (12%), S(40%), and G2(22%) arrested cells, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B, C.

claim: 40% of the arrest regulated proteins peak in S arrested cells.
source: This identified four clusters (Figure 2B,C), each showing peak protein abundance at different cell cycle phases, that is, proteins that peak in G0/G1 (12%), S(40%), and G2(22%) arrested cells, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B, C.

claim: 22% of the arrest regulated proteins peak in G2 arrested cells.
source: This identified four clusters (Figure 2B,C), each showing peak protein abundance at different cell cycle phases, that is, proteins that peak in G0/G1 (12%), S(40%), and G2(22%) arrested cells, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B, C.

claim: The fourth cluster (26%) contains proteins that show their lowest abundance in S phase.
source: The fourth cluster (26%) contains proteins that show their lowest abundance in S phase.

claim: In the elutriated cell system, ~50% of the changing proteome peaked at G2&M phases.
source: These data differ from the results obtained for the same NB4 cell line using elutriated cells in the 'minimally perturbed' system, where ∼50% of the changing proteome in elutriated cells peaked at G2&M phases (Figure 5 in Ly et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Figure 5 in Ly et al., 2014.

claim: The G0/G1-peaking cluster is enriched in chromatin assembly and cholesterol biosynthesis proteins.
source: Analysis of gene ontology (GO) terms associated with each of the four clusters (Figure 2B), shows that the G0/G1-peaking cluster is enriched in chromatin assembly and cholesterol biosynthesis proteins, the S-peaking cluster is enriched in ribosome biosynthesis and translation proteins, the G2-peaking cluster is enriched in cell division proteins and the S-minimum cluster is enriched in redox and lipid modification proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The S-peaking cluster is enriched in ribosome biosynthesis and translation proteins.
source: Analysis of gene ontology (GO) terms associated with each of the four clusters (Figure 2B), shows that the G0/G1-peaking cluster is enriched in chromatin assembly and cholesterol biosynthesis proteins, the S-peaking cluster is enriched in ribosome biosynthesis and translation proteins, the G2-peaking cluster is enriched in cell division proteins and the S-minimum cluster is enriched in redox and lipid modification proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The G2-peaking cluster is enriched in cell division proteins.
source: Analysis of gene ontology (GO) terms associated with each of the four clusters (Figure 2B), shows that the G0/G1-peaking cluster is enriched in chromatin assembly and cholesterol biosynthesis proteins, the S-peaking cluster is enriched in ribosome biosynthesis and translation proteins, the G2-peaking cluster is enriched in cell division proteins and the S-minimum cluster is enriched in redox and lipid modification proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The S-minimum cluster is enriched in redox and lipid modification proteins.
source: Analysis of gene ontology (GO) terms associated with each of the four clusters (Figure 2B), shows that the G0/G1-peaking cluster is enriched in chromatin assembly and cholesterol biosynthesis proteins, the S-peaking cluster is enriched in ribosome biosynthesis and translation proteins, the G2-peaking cluster is enriched in cell division proteins and the S-minimum cluster is enriched in redox and lipid modification proteins.

claim: Of the 484 cell cycle arrest regulated proteins, only 212 correlate well (Pearson's correlation coefficient ≥0.50) with the patterns measured for proteins in the elutriated cell system.
source: Of the 484 cell cycle arrest regulated proteins, only 212 correlate well (Pearson's correlation coefficient ≥0.50) with the patterns measured for proteins in the elutriated cell system (212/453, representing 47% of the union between the two data sets) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison between the two datasets.

claim: The proteins that correlate well between the two datasets are highly enriched in genes annotated with functions in cellular division, for example, CDC20, Aurora Kinase B, and mitotic kinesins.
source: The proteins that correlate well between the two datasets are highly enriched in genes annotated with functions in cellular division, for example, CDC20, Aurora Kinase B, and mitotic kinesins.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the proteins that correlate between datasets.

claim: Of the 212 proteins that correlate well between datasets, only 29/212 (14%) change by more than twofold in both the cell cycle arrest and elutriated cell cycle datasets.
source: Of these, only 29/212 (14%) change by more than twofold in both the cell cycle arrest and elutriated cell cycle datasets.

claim: In both datasets, MT–ND5 peaks in G1 and G2.
source: For example, in both datasets the mitochondrial genome-encoded protein MT–ND5 peaks in G1 and G2, while RRM2, TK1, and CCNB1 (cyclin B1) are lowest in abundance in G1, and peak in S and G2&M (Figure 2D).

claim: In both datasets, RRM2, TK1, and CCNB1 (cyclin B1) are lowest in abundance in G1, and peak in S and G2&M.
source: For example, in both datasets the mitochondrial genome-encoded protein MT–ND5 peaks in G1 and G2, while RRM2, TK1, and CCNB1 (cyclin B1) are lowest in abundance in G1, and peak in S and G2&M (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Proteins showing cell cycle regulation in abundance can be detected using either an arrest or a minimally perturbing elutriation strategy.
source: While this indicates that proteins showing cell cycle regulation in abundance can be detected using either an arrest, or a minimally perturbing, elutriation strategy, it also highlights the major differences between these experimental systems.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the comparison of the two datasets.

claim: Most proteins that were detected to change in abundance upon cell cycle arrest (53%) do not show cell cycle variation in their abundance in cells analyzed by elutriation.
source: It is striking that most proteins that were detected here to change in abundance upon cell cycle arrest (53%) do not show cell cycle variation in their abundance in cells analysed by elutriation.

claim: Most of the proteins whose abundances change upon serum starvation do not show cell cycle stage variations in abundance in elutriated cells.
source: To explore this further, we examined the protein networks and signaling pathways that changed specifically upon each cell cycle arrest. Most of the proteins whose abundances change upon serum starvation do not show cell cycle stage variations in abundance in elutriated cells.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison between the two datasets.

claim: Changes specific to the serum starvation arrest protocol include a dramatic increase in the levels of proteins involved in cellular metabolism.
source: Changes specific to the serum starvation arrest protocol include a dramatic increase in the levels of proteins involved in cellular metabolism (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Many proteins that increase upon serum starvation are involved in catabolic pathways and in the generation of precursor and/or secondary metabolites.
source: Many are involved in catabolic pathways and in the generation of precursor and/or secondary metabolites.

claim: The FAHD2A, GCDH, and BCKDHB genes all encode proteins important for the catabolism of amino acids.
source: For example, the FAHD2A, GCDH, and BCKDHB genes all encode proteins important for the catabolism of amino acids.

claim: Another major change to metabolism upon serum starvation is the increase in abundance of cholesterol biosynthesis enzymes.
source: Another major change to metabolism upon serum starvation is the increase in abundance of cholesterol biosynthesis enzymes.

claim: 42% (5/12) of the quantitated cholesterol biosynthesis enzymes increase by more than twofold upon serum starvation.

claim: Serum starvation of human fibroblasts has been shown to induce increased transcription of sterol metabolism genes, such as HMGCS1, through transcriptional activation by SREBP.

claim: Serum starvation induces significant changes in the abundance of chromatin components and chromatin remodelers.
source: Serum starvation also induces significant changes in the abundance of chromatin components and chromatin remodelers, as shown in a network diagram of chromatin and chromatin-associated proteins that significantly change upon serum starvation (Figure 3C).

claim: Proteins in the nucleosome core, for example, histones H2A (HIST1H2AJ), H3.1 (HIST1H3A), and H4 (HIST1H4A), and the variant histone H2A.Z (H2AFX), are all upregulated upon serum starvation.

claim: Serum starvation has an unanticipated effect in modulating total histone levels.

claim: Serum starvation induces major changes affecting chromatin that are not observed during normal cell cycle progression, as judged from the elutriated cells.

source: Hydroxyurea arrests cells in S-phase by depleting deoxynucleotide levels and slowing replication (Alvino et al., 2007).
